course_details.Meeting Info: Kresge Centennial Hall 2-343: Mon, Wed, Fri 3:00PM - 3:50PM
course_details.Overview of class:
What is it like speaking Spanish in the U.S.? An exploration of language and raciolinguistic ideologies

This writing seminar examines the intersections between language, identity, race, and power through the lived experiences of Spanish-speaking communities in the United States. Drawing on sociolinguistic and critical perspectives, we will explore how historical, social, and political forces have shaped perceptions of Spanish and its speakers, and how language ideologies are (re)produced and challenged through everyday discourse and institutional practices. Topics include the sociohistorical context of Spanish in the U.S., bilingualism, linguistic discrimination, racialization, language and identity, and inequalities in education.

Throughout the quarter, students will engage critically with academic readings and multimodal materials, including videos, podcasts, and examples of public discourse. Class discussions and collaborative activities will encourage students to examine different scholarly perspectives, question taken-for-granted assumptions about language, and connect theoretical concepts to everyday experiences.

As a writing seminar, the course emphasizes critical literacy, evidence-based argumentation, and academic writing development. Students will complete two analytical essays: a linguistic autoethnography examining their own language histories and identities, and an argumentative essay investigating language ideologies within their academic fields. They will also collaborate on a linguistic landscape project to examine how languages are represented and valued in public spaces. Writing workshops, peer feedback, and revision will be integrated throughout the quarter to help students develop their analytical skills and academic voice.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
- Critically analyze language ideologies: Identify and critically examine how beliefs about language, race, and identity shape perceptions of Spanish-speaking communities and influence social and institutional practices in the United States.

- Apply sociolinguistic and raciolinguistic perspectives: Use key course concepts to analyze personal linguistic experiences, educational contexts, and representations of language in public spaces, connecting individual experiences to broader historical, social, and political structures.

- Construct evidence-based arguments: Develop clear, organized, and well-supported written arguments by critically evaluating, synthesizing, and integrating evidence from academic readings and other relevant sources.

- Make intentional rhetorical choices: Analyze how authors use language, style, and rhetorical strategies for different audiences and purposes, and apply these insights to develop their own academic writing and voice.

- Engage in writing as a process: Plan, draft, evaluate, and revise academic writing using peer and instructor feedback to strengthen the clarity, organization, and effectiveness of their arguments.

- Collaborative critical inquiry: Engage in constructive academic dialogue by discussing complex ideas, responding to differing perspectives, and providing evidence-based feedback to peers.

course_details.Learning Objectives:
Specific Spanish 205-0 Course Goals
• Further develop communicative and cultural competence within the medical context of the Spanishspeaking
world.
• Ability to utilize problem-solving skills, advocate the communication process, solicit and take down accurate
information while conducting interviews with Spanish speakers.
• Ability to research and present concrete and factual health topics and/or diseases in formal and informal
situations.
• Expand student's functional vocabulary, in particular, the language and colloquial terms Hispanics use in
medical settings.
• Develop a greater understanding of Hispanic cultural medical practices, the patient-doctor relationship and
common home remedies used to treat illnesses.
• Gain greater insights of the needs and problems that many Hispanics and health care institutions face due
to a language barrier.

Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course, students will:
• Handle a variety of communicative tasks using the past, present, and future tenses, as well as complex
tenses and grammatical structures. Errors rarely interfere with communication.
• Speak in a natural and continuous speech; use of connectors to link sentences into paragraph-length
discourse.
• Express and support ideas based on the information studied, as well as to express agreement or
disagreement to interlocutor's arguments, and express counter points effectively and persuasively.
• Have control of common, general vocabulary, and some use of specialized medical terminology.
• Write work with few errors in agreement, punctuation, etc.
• Articulate arguments justified with examples, counter-examples, and real information, in formal and
informal discourse.

course_name: The Novel in Latin America: Society, State, Nature (Taught in English)

course_info.course_name: The Novel in Latin America: Society, State, Nature (Taught in English)

course_details.Meeting Info: Kresge Centennial Hall 2-319: Mon, Wed 9:00AM - 9:50AM
course_details.Overview of class: Can novels help us understand what Latin America means now and what it has meant in the past? Can they help us understand what the world beyond the region means? This course will examine the modern Latin American novel in terms of three of its obsessions: society, state, and nature. We will explore canonical—and blockbuster—novels of the so-called Boom period with an eye to their elaborate articulations of the region, its inhabitants and their identities. Beyond proposals of magical realities, we will focus on the ways in which identity becomes a point of resolution and problem for understanding Latin American societies as well as, crucially, grasping the region's place in global history. We will also interrogate the way in which these novels, at times anachronistically, undercut the fixation on identity by introducing doubts concerning nationalism, the individual, class hierarchies, capitalism and, especially, the way in which these have intersected with the state in the region. We will pay special attention to what, if anything, is "Latin American" about these novels. Finally, we will read a novel from the same period that, turning away from what one critic has called "mestizo-criollo-elite" literary practices, leaves behind simplifying representations of nature as anti-civilization in order to claim the natural broadly conceived as a site of knowledge and epistemology. Importantly, it hinges on the centrality of indigenous peoples and indigeneity not to regional identity but rather to a redefinition of what we understand humanity to be and how it has been defined in Latin American and world history. course_details.Overview of class:
In the United States, we often talk about Latinx people using blurry labels. We discuss the Latino vote, the Hispanic population, and the Latinx community. This course explores the nuances of these labels through the stories that Latinx authors have been narrating for the past six decades. As we follow characters through conflicts and inhabit their quotidian lives, we will navigate between the specificity of a story and the complexity of a Latinx identity. Class discussions will study emotional ties to places and languages, feminist thought, and the racial and ethnic diversity within the Latinx community. We will read authors such as Gloria Anzaldúa, Justin Torres, Helena Maria Viramontes, and Yxta Maya Murray.

A one-quarter course cannot do justice to the rich genealogy of Latinx writing. This course follows an illustrative sample of authors from the 1970s onward and focuses on short stories, poetry, and essays. It aims to provide students with a historical, political, and literary foundation for further exploration of Latinx literature.(Taught in English)

This course explores the rich and vibrant traditions of contemporary Indigenous storytelling and their relationship to the short story genre. We will engage with a diverse array of stories written, told, and performed by Yucatec Maya, Mapuche, Quechua, and other Indigenous authors, situating each work within its own cultural and historical context. Through this comparative approach, we will explore the ways Indigenous storytellers challenge conventional literary categories and expand our understanding of what constitutes a short story. course_details.Overview of class:
Women Who Kill: Criminality and Gender in Latin American Culture

In Women Who Kill: Criminality and Gender in Latin American Culture, we will confront the unsettling figure of the woman who kills—whether she murders, is murdered, or turns violence upon herself—as a mirror through which Latin American culture reveals its deepest anxieties about law, justice, and gender. What does it mean for a woman to kill in a world where the law, medicine, and literature have long defined her as victim, patient, or saint? How do acts of female violence—real or symbolic—unsettle social order and expose the patriarchal structures that sustain it?
Spanning from the late 19th century to the present, this course examines how literature and film transform women's transgression into a space for reimagining justice, power, and representation. By tracing stories of real and fictional women who kill, we will interrogate the fragile boundaries between justice and vengeance, sanity and hysteria, the private and the public—rethinking how gender and law shape one another within cultural discourse. Readings will include works by Juana Manuela Gorriti, Emilia Pardo Bazán, Jorge Luis Borges, Roberto Bolaño, Mariana Enriquez, Ariel Dorfman, and Alia Trabucco Zerán. Prerequisite: 1 course from SPANISH 250-0, SPANISH 251-0, SPANISH 260-0, or SPANISH 261-0.
course_details.Learning Objectives: This course aims to develop a critical understanding of how women who kill are represented in Latin American literature and culture, tracing these portrayals from the 19th century to today. Students will explore the intersections of gender, law, and justice, analyzing how female criminality challenges and reshapes social norms, legal frameworks, and cultural narratives. Through close engagement with diverse texts—including literature and film—students will deepen their ability to interpret themes related to gendered violence, power, and resistance within historical and political contexts. Additionally, the course fosters skills in critical discussion and collaborative analysis, encouraging students to articulate their insights both orally and in creative group projects that integrate digital media tools.

course_details.Overview of class:
Dystopian Latin America: Literature and Film after 1990

Dystopia is everywhere. From Marvel blockbusters to daily headlines warning of ecological collapse driven by extractive industries, we are constantly exposed to dire visions of the future. In Latin America, dystopia has long been more than a spectacle of catastrophe; it is a sharp critique of the present that still holds onto utopian hope, that is, the belief that collective resistance can avert disaster and imagine better worlds. Latin American dystopias channel anxieties born of histories of authoritarianism, racial violence, and environmental devastation, while protesting against futures of dispossession. This course offers an overview of dystopian imaginaries across Latin America through short stories, films and TV series. We will explore ecological, political, and racial dystopias to understand how these narratives articulate our deepest fears and anxieties, but also how they gesture toward alternatives rooted in communal memory, solidarity, and imagination. Prerequisite: 1 course from SPANISH 250-0, SPANISH 251-0, SPANISH 260-0, or SPANISH 261-0.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
• Familiarize yourself with different definitions and expressions of dystopia.
• Compare how dystopias articulate present anxieties in different parts of Latin America.
• Identify the tools dystopias offer to creatively think about how to prevent future crises.
• Develop the ability to close read literary and cinematic texts
